claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC state.
Residual-stress relief during post-cooling annealing governs phase stability.
Enhanced local solute diffusion at dislocations and grain boundaries governs phase stability.
Stress relief and defect-assisted solute diffusion promote heterogeneous nucleation of secondary phases from the metastable BCC matrix.
Intermediate-temperature annealing can induce stress relief and solute segregation relative to rapid quenching.
The mechanism requires an annealing temperature and duration sufficient for appreciable atomic diffusion and internal-stress relaxation.
The applicable annealing regime lies below the stability range of the high-temperature BCC phase.
Very rapid cooling suppresses diffusion and therefore suppresses the proposed mechanism.
Exposure at sufficiently high temperature maintains BCC stability and prevents the proposed mechanism from applying.
Annealing relaxes residual stress and reduces dislocation density.
Annealing promotes localized solute clustering at grain boundaries and other defect sites.
Reduced dislocation density and localized solute clustering lower the nucleation-energy barrier.
The lowered nucleation barrier causes heterogeneous formation and growth of ordered or FCC-like secondary phases within the BCC matrix.
Annealed samples will contain a larger measurable secondary-phase fraction than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will retain more metastable BCC material and form fewer secondary phases than annealed samples.
Rapid quenching retains high residual stress.
When atomic mobility is negligible, no significant phase transformation occurs and the BCC phase is retained.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes enhanced diffusion and heterogeneous nucleation at dislocations, while the mechanism says annealing reduces dislocation density and treats that reduction as part of what lowers the nucleation barrier. The account does not resolve how removing proposed nucleation and diffusion sites promotes defect-mediated nucleation.
